opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the opportunity is really significant, partly because the gap right now is so stark. Most of the breakthroughs we've seen in large language models have been concentrated in a handful of languages, overwhelmingly English. That's not because other languages matter less. It's a reflection of where the data is, where the compute is, and frankly where the researchers are. So you end up with this situation where a huge fraction of the world's population is interacting with technology that simply doesn't work as well for them, or doesn't work at all.

What excites me about Aya is that we approached it as a question of who gets to participate in building these systems, not just which languages are covered. We set it up as an open science effort, so we had a very large community of researchers and native speakers from all over the world contributing. People weren't just annotators. They were collaborators who understood the nuances of their own languages and cultures in a way no centralized team could replicate.

A lot of the work went into the data, especially instruction-style data. If you want a model to follow instructions well in Yoruba or Telugu or Turkish, you need high-quality examples of that. You can't just translate English prompts and hope the cultural context carries over. Often it doesn't. So a big part of the project was creating and curating data that reflects how people actually speak and what they actually care about.

There are real technical challenges too. When you train on many languages at once, you run into what we sometimes call the curse of multilinguality. Capacity gets spread thin, and you have to think carefully about how you balance languages so you don't help one at the expense of another. Evaluation is another big problem. Most of our benchmarks are English-centric, so even measuring progress in other languages takes deliberate work.

But I think the bigger picture is this: if we only optimize these models for a small slice of the world, we're baking in a very narrow view of what intelligence and usefulness look like. Expanding beyond English isn't just about fairness, though that matters a great deal. It also makes the research better, because it forces us to confront assumptions we didn't realize we were making. For me, that's the real opportunity.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks so much for having me, Sam. It's great to be back.

I think the way I frame Aya is that it started from a very simple observation that was, frankly, a bit uncomfortable for our field. We've had this remarkable wave of progress in generative AI over the last few years, but if you look at who that progress has actually served, it's overwhelmingly been English speakers, and to a lesser extent a handful of other high-resource languages. There are roughly seven thousand languages spoken in the world, and the vast majority of them are either completely absent from these models or represented so poorly that the models are effectively unusable for those speakers. So you have billions of people who are, in a very real sense, on the outside of this technology looking in.

And what's striking is that the gap isn't really a modeling problem in the narrow sense. The architectures work. Transformers don't care what language you feed them. The bottleneck is data, specifically high-quality instruction data, the kind of examples that teach a model how to actually follow a request and be useful. For English, we have an abundance of that. For Yoruba or Kyrgyz or Sinhala, there's close to nothing. And you can't just machine translate your way out of it, because translation introduces its own artifacts and loses the cultural grounding that makes a model feel like it actually belongs to a community rather than being imported into it.

So the opportunity with Aya was really twofold. The first was to build the dataset that didn't exist. We ended up with about three thousand collaborators across more than a hundred countries, many of them native speakers, linguists, people who cared deeply about their languages being represented. That produced the largest multilingual instruction collection that's been released, covering over a hundred languages, with a large portion of it human-annotated rather than synthetic. The second was to show what you could do with it, by releasing a model trained on that data openly, so that researchers and developers in those communities could build on it rather than waiting for a frontier lab to decide their language was commercially interesting.

But I'd say the thing I'm most excited about goes beyond any single dataset or model. What Aya demonstrated, to me, is a different way of doing this kind of research. Most large-scale AI efforts are built in a very centralized way by a small number of people in a few cities. Aya was built by a distributed community, and that matters not just for coverage but for quality. The people who understand what "good" looks like in a given language are the people who speak it. When you bring them into the process as collaborators rather than treating them as a data source to be mined, you get something fundamentally richer. And it also changes who gets to see themselves as part of the field.

There's also a research dimension that I think is underappreciated. Multilingual models are a fantastic lens for understanding how these systems generalize. When you train on a hundred languages, you start to see interesting transfer effects, you see where capabilities are shared across languages and where they're not, and you confront questions about tokenization, about evaluation, about safety in languages where the model has seen very little data. Those are hard problems, and they don't get solved if everyone keeps optimizing for English benchmarks.

So I'd say the opportunity is both practical and intellectual. Practically, it's about making sure this technology serves most of humanity rather than a small slice of it. Intellectually, it's about expanding what we even consider the frontier to be. Right now the frontier is defined almost entirely in terms of scale and English-language performance. I think a more honest definition of progress would ask whether a model can be useful to someone in Lagos or Dhaka or La Paz in the language they actually think in. And we're really just at the beginning of that.

astra-6.text:
I think the opportunity is enormous. When we talk about breakthroughs in generative AI, we have to ask: breakthroughs for whom? If you can only really benefit from these systems in English, then a huge number of people are left out of that progress.

With Aya, the opportunity is to make multilingual capability a central goal. And that takes more than translating English examples. Language carries culture, context, and different ways of expressing what matters. You need people who speak those languages to help shape what useful behavior looks like and how you evaluate it.

That’s what makes the community aspect so exciting to me. It creates an opportunity for people to participate in building this technology, rather than simply receiving something designed elsewhere. The ambition is for someone to interact with a model in their own language and have it be useful on their terms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is enormous. Language shapes who can participate in these breakthroughs, and if we build primarily for English, we leave out so much of the world’s knowledge and experience.

With Aya, the question is: how do we make progress across languages by bringing people into the process who actually speak those languages? It’s not simply translating English data. You need people who can tell you whether a response is useful, whether it sounds natural, and whether it makes sense in their cultural context.

And that’s an exciting research challenge as well. How do we help languages where there’s less data available? How do we measure progress when our evaluation tools are uneven? For me, the opportunity is to broaden both who benefits from generative AI and who gets to shape it.
